To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
postponement of childrearing is associated with a) the educational system, b) the labour market, and c) housing markets.

the postponement of childrearing is a major contributing cause of low fertility in low-fertility countries; and, the postponement of childbirth can be reversed through policy changes in the education system, the labour markets, and the housing markets.
the postponement in fertility is a result of changes in the transition to adulthood and that these changes are a result of institutional factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of institutions and policies in shaping the timing of childrearing and, by implication, fertility.
the question of how to increase fertility in low-fertility countries.
the question: How might institutions and policies be altered to encourage younger childbearing?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of any major changes in the institutions and policies discussed above, fertility will continue to be postponed.

the more the transition to adulthood is prolonged, the more difficult it is to integrate childbearing into a career, and the more difficult it becomes to enter the housing market, the later childbearing will occur.
the more the institutions in a society facilitate a smooth transition to adulthood and the easier it is to combine work and childrearing, the earlier childbearing is likely to occur.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transition to adulthood is becoming increasingly prolonged, and that this is a significant factor in postponement of child-bearing in many countries.

the institutions that facilitate childbearing and childrearing in the first place, such as the educational system, the housing market and the labour market, also facilitate childbearing and, in particular, childbearing at younger ages.
the postponement and tempo of fertility are not only about the desire to have children but also about the desire for a good job and a good home.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the timing of childrearing is an outcome, and that policy makers should not be concerned with the timing per se, but rather with how it is achieved.
policy discussions about fertility should include a discussion about the transition to adulthood, as well as a discussion about the timing of childrearing.
policy discussions should not focus exclusively on increasing fertility rates.
